query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid free energy workflow that integrates a machine‐learned interatomic potential—trained on a strategically small set of ab initio molecular dynamics data capturing vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling—can yield accurate fusion and high‐temperature thermodynamic properties for both solid and liquid states while reducing computational cost by an order of magnitude compared to explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD methods, even for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloy systems at high temperatures near melting/fusion conditions.
generation.intervention: Deploy a hybrid ML-based free energy integration framework that uses sparse ab initio MD simulations to train a surrogate potential which faithfully reproduces the key many-body and anharmonic interactions affecting free energies.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed under high-temperature conditions (typically ≥1000 K up to the melting point) in both solid and fluid states and under pressures relevant to fusion environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The machine-learned surrogate potential, which mediates the mapping from limited ab initio data to an accurate yet computationally inexpensive representation of interatomic interactions.
generation.mechanism: By training on a minimal set of high-fidelity MD trajectories, the surrogate potential captures the crucial vibrational entropy, anharmonic fluctuations, and electron–vibration coupling that determine the free energy landscape. This allows for efficient thermodynamic integration without the need for extensive full ab initio MD sampling, thereby drastically reducing computational requirements.
generation.predicted_outcome: The proposed method should substantially reduce computational expense—potentially by an order of magnitude—while maintaining free energy accuracy within experimental or high-fidelity simulation uncertainty. However, uncertainties remain regarding the transferability of the learned potential to chemically complex, multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD methods that require dense sampling for accurate free energy evaluations.
generation.boundary: Applicable to systems where both solid and liquid phases are present under high-temperature (fusion-relevant) conditions; its effectiveness in systems with extreme chemical disorder or outside these temperature/pressure ranges remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty as to whether the surrogate potential can universally capture all relevant entropy contributions (especially in highly disordered, multicomponent systems) and maintain fidelity across different compositional spaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the hybrid ML-enhanced free energy integration method to two systems: (1) a well-characterized binary alloy (e.g., an Al-Cu system) and (2) a representative multicomponent high-entropy alloy. Compute the free energy differences of solid and liquid phases at fusion-relevant temperatures and compare these predictions against results obtained from full ab initio MD simulations and established experimental melting data.
measurements: Vibrational entropy and other relevant entropy contributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-enhanced method fails to predict free energy differences and derived fusion properties within the accepted uncertainty bounds of full ab initio MD benchmarks or does not achieve at least a tenfold reduction in computational cost relative to TOR-TILD or full ab initio MD methods, then the hypothesis is falsified.

RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . A key component in current tokamak designs is the divertor, which will be in contact with the deuterium-tritium (D-T) plasma and sustain severe fluxes of particles (helium (He) ash, D and T) and heat, along with radiation damage induced by high-energy neutrons [2] , [3] . Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.
